extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics, historians of mathematics, and mathematicians interested in foundations and methodology (graduate students and researchers)
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and evaluation of the 'purity of method' in mathematical proofs and foundational investigations, especially as exemplified in Hilbert's work on geometry. The task concerns judging when certain methods are appropriate, necessary, or epistemically preferable and how such judgements motivate foundational (e.g., independence/impossibility) results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topical purity (purity as symmetry between proof-resources and content)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideal of topical purity enforces a certain symmetry between the conceptual resources used to prove a theorem and those needed for the clarification of its content: 'the resources of proof ought ideally to be restricted to those which determine its content.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purity here means restricting proof methods to those that belong to the topic of the theorem. Motives for this ideal vary (epistemic vs pragmatic). Examples discussed include searches for purely elementary proofs (Erdős–Mordell), algebraic proofs replacing model-theoretic ones (Gilmer & Mott), and measure-theoretic results proved without appeal to measure theory beyond definitions (Woo). The ideal can be treated as an epistemic demand (gives the most basic reasons why a proposition is true) or as a pragmatic/strategic one (improves pedagogical efficiency and community division of labor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hilbert's 'basic principle' (elucidate possibility/impossibility with restricted methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: One ought to elucidate given problems in such a way as to decide whether they can be answered 'in a prescribed way with certain restricted methods', and, if not, to recognise the grounds for the impossibility of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle grounds investigations into impossibility/unprovability (Abel on quintic, independence of the Parallel Axiom, Lindemann on e and π). It functions as a general prescription governing searches for mathematical knowledge: establish whether particular methods suffice and, if not, demonstrate impossibility so as to advance understanding or open up new domains of research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess whether a method is 'appropriate' to the subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Question whether it is 'appropriate' to use certain domains or methods (e.g., complex function theory in number theory, transfinite numbers in analysis) when proving theorems in a given subject area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This involves asking whether the use of external methods is necessary or merely expedient and whether apparent cross-domain connections are accidental or reflect deeper theoretical reasons. Hilbert suggests that judgements about appropriateness are often subjective and that the 'right' approach may depend on purposes; he recommends gathering information (e.g., possibility/necessity results) to place such questions on an objective footing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate necessity of methods and deeper versus accidental connections
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask whether a certain theorem can only be proved by using extended theoretical means, or whether the connections established by such methods are accidental or have deeper theoretical reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Answering these questions motivates foundational work: search for proofs, independence results, or reductions that show necessity or dispensability of methods. The text recommends critical analysis to determine whether cross-domain techniques indicate genuine conceptual links or are avoidable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purity investigations as analysis of the 'logical weight' of axioms and the necessity of assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Foundational investigations should determine which axioms, assumptions or auxiliary means are necessary in the proof of a given elementary geometrical truth and assess their 'logical weight'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert's program groups axioms (e.g., incidence, order, congruence vs. parallels, Archimedean) and uses independence results to show different levels of empirical/intuitive support. Purity analysis therefore includes isolating minimal axiom sets for particular theorems and clarifying which assumptions are essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impossibility/unprovability proofs as fully satisfactory solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Proving the impossibility (unprovability) of solving a problem by certain means counts as a 'fully satisfactory and rigorous solution' of the problem, albeit in a different sense than a constructive proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert regards demonstrations of unprovability as important and fruitful outcomes that advance knowledge: they settle whether the intended method can succeed, and their pursuit can stimulate discovery of new domains. Examples include squaring the circle, solvability of quintics, and independence of parallels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purity as pragmatic/epistemic instrument (discipline, pedagogy, division of labor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Purity is often prized not only for intrinsic epistemic superiority but for pragmatic epistemic ends: as 'good discipline for the mind', for pedagogical efficiency, and for improving community epistemic efficiency by making theorems usable by specialists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purity reduces conceptual overhead between definitions and demonstrations (pedagogic efficiency), trains mathematical thinking (mental discipline), and creates cleaner interfaces between specialties so results can be productively used by those best positioned to exploit them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group axioms by empirical/experimental justificatory character
rubrics_metrics.description: Axioms may differ in their empirical or intuitive character; for example, incidence, order, and congruence axioms have simpler, more directly demonstrable experimental grounding than the Parallel or Archimedean axioms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purity/foundational work should recognise these differences: independence results show that some axioms require separate justificatory support. Hilbert treats such distinctions as part of assessing the proper sources of geometrical knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject the means of proof to critical analysis (allowing but interrogating cross-domain methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: One should subject the means of carrying out a proof to critical analysis, questioning appeals to other domains (e.g., using geometry in arithmetic proofs or function theory in geometry) while acknowledging such mixtures can reveal 'beautiful and fruitful relations'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical analysis does not mandate forbidding cross-domain methods; rather, it seeks to understand when such methods are indispensable, when they are pedagogically or epistemically preferable, and when they indicate deeper theoretical connections worth exploring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Project onto the 'conceptual level' — purity results as producing abstract/logical outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Purity investigations often yield abstract mathematical/logical results at a conceptual level that can 'emancipate' mathematics from epistemological constraints about what is 'appropriate'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond assessing appropriateness, purity results can produce higher-level conceptual insights (e.g., logical/structural results) which are essential to what is attained by purity investigations; such outcomes may justify mixing domains even while clarifying the foundational picture.
